speechtext:
That this House call upon the government to recognize that Canada's municipal infrastructure is facing a crisis of national proportions and that, given the serious implications to the nation's environment, economic prosperity and quality of life for Canadians, the government resume its traditional role as a partner with the provincial and municipal governments to address this national crisis.
He said: Madam Speaker, I want to thank our House leader for giving me the opportunity to speak on this very important issue today.
This issue has a tremendous impact on the cities, towns and villages which make up our country. Municipal infrastructure is not very glamorous, but it is absolutely vital to the health and vitality of our national environment and economy.
The motion we have tabled today calls upon the government to recognize this very simple, but extremely important fact. I would like to acknowledge at the very outset the tremendous work being done on this issue by the Federation of Canadian Municipalities. We thank them for taking a leadership role and speaking out on behalf of Canadian towns and cities.
Their research and well-documented studies have enabled us to make sense out of a very complex issue.
I cannot think of a segment of our lives not touched on a daily basis by municipal infrastructure. When people ask what is infrastructure, I think that before we even arrive at work in the morning we have probably showered, flushed the toilet, used the water from the kitchen tap to make coffee, and driven on paved roadways to our job that would not exist if it were not for services provided by local infrastructure.
Whether we live in big cities or in small towns, infrastructure provides the basis for our homes, our jobs, our standard of living, and the maintenance of our own environment.
For many years we were able to take these services for granted, and we did. Government at all levels turned away from building bridges and repairing roads and concentrated on what some call soft infrastructure, such as social services which also have become an integral part of the Canadian way of life.
Now we have used up the extra capacity that was built into the infrastructure in the first half of this century. The sewers, roads, bridges and sidewalks can no longer cope with the ever-increasing demands.
Often discussion on this issue turns into debates on who is responsible. Time and energy are wasted as politicians argue back and forth accusing each other. What I would like to say today is that there is no longer any time to debate who is responsible. We must accept the fact that we have a national crisis on our hands, a crisis that requires national recognition and assistance. The municipalities simply cannot do it alone.
As a former alderman I learned a great deal about the challenges facing municipal government, and this past year as co-chairman of the National Liberal Task Force on Municipal Infrastructure I was able to witness first hand just how serious this situation is in our country.
My colleague from Nepean and I visited towns where raw sewage flowed down open ditches. We heard from villages where residents must import fresh water. For

May 25, 1990

example, on the east coast of this country we witnessed raw sewage being dumped directly into the ocean. A similar scene greeted us on the west coast.
Canadians along the Trans-Canada Highway reported ever-increasing accidents due to a badly deteriorating national road system. We heard from developers who are trying to fill a need for affordable housing but who are frustrated because of the inadequate infrastructure available to them.
In one municipality in New Brunswick we heard about an industrial park that was developed to promote economic development in this region where unemployment levels are reaching serious proportions. Unfortunately, so far the industrial park has no water supply. It is rather discouraging, Madam Speaker, for businesses that are thinking about locating there.

Since some of the oldest Canadian municipalities are in Quebec, it is not surprising that their infrastructure requirements are rapidly approaching a critical stage.
The dumping of sewage and untreated water into the St. Lawrence, which has gone on for centuries, has devastated this waterway that plays a vital role. According to the urban communities of Quebec, 500 million litres of untreated water and 50 metric tons of raw sewage are dumped into the river every day. Madam Speaker, that is as much as three times the capacity of the Quebec coliseum or the contents of 15,000 garbage trucks.
Besides this environmental nightmare, many municipalities located along the highways leading to the rural recreation areas of the province in the Laurentians and the Ottawa Valley say that they fear the influx of non-residents will contribute to the deterioration of roads and local services. These municipalities, which do not have the increased revenues of the tourist centres, must still absorb additional costs due to their proximity to these resorts.

Obviously, Madam Speaker, municipal needs are no longer a subject for discussion only at town council meetings. It has come up time and time again at environmental conferences, at the board tables of corporations, in housing reports, and in transportation studies.
How does municipal infrastructure affect us on a national level?
Let us look for a moment at the issues before us today at the national level: first, a growing concern about the environment; second, real fears about the economy and our ability to compete in tough international markets; third, a monumental national debt and increases in inflation, interest rates, and unemployment levels; and, fourth, serious regional economic development and serious regional economic disparities which limit employment opportunities and force the migration of Canadians away from their homes and into already crowded urban centres simply to make a living.
It is my firm belief that in the middle of these issues and central both to the cause and their cure is the urgent need to rebuild and upgrade Canada's municipal infrastructure.
I would first like to outline the relationship between the environment and the municipal infrastructure. Canadians have ranked the environment as their top priority for federal action. The growing concern about the mistreatment of our greatest national resource, our environment, has prompted a wide variety of action on the part of all levels of government.
Canadians want us to save our waterways. They want us to stop polluting our land and our air. They want an assurance that their governments at all levels are safeguarding the inheritance of their children by following policies based on sustainable development. However, a quick look at some of the basic facts tell us pretty quickly that this is not what we are doing at all.
For example, Environment Canada figures tell us that only 10 per cent of all raw sewage east of Ontario goes through a treatment process. We also know that more than 8 million Canadians or one-third of our population live in municipalities without sewage treatment.
In Newfoundland, for example, over 48,000 homes do not have adequate water or sewer services, and 80 per cent of the population does not have properly treated drinking water.
In Toronto, as another example, the water quality is so bad that some politicians are calling for a $200 million pipeline from Georgian Bay.
Canadians are spending millions of dollars every year on bottled water, which is not surprising when we stop to consider that in many parts of Canada eating fish caught
May 25, 1990

in lakes and rivers which are sources of drinking water is actually dangerous to human health.
In my riding of Ottawa Centre and across this country beaches are being closed because of unsafe levels of pollution. We are surrounded by water and yet told that we cannot swim in it or eat the fish. Our children are growing up in a world very different from the one we knew. Unfortunately, the environmental damage caused by municipal infrastructure is not limited to our waterways. The deplorable condition of the Trans-Canada Highway and a vast number of provincial and municipal roads is also hurting our environment.
We know carbon dioxide emissions hurt our air quality and contribute to global warming, and we recognize this as a national and international problem. We have unfortunately failed to make the connection between bad roads and air pollution, but the Canadian Automobile Association has made that connection. It estimates that 10.3 per cent of carbon dioxide emissions come from automobile travel. Travelling roads in poor condition uses more fuel than when roads are properly maintained and results in higher levels of emissions.
In Ontario, for example, vehicle registrations have risen by 85 per cent. Yet, using the province's own standards, as many as 50 per cent of the roads these cars are using will soon be listed in fair to poor condition.
The severe cut-backs to VIA Rail passenger service has also dealt a blow to the environment. By forcing more Canadians into individual cars, which must then travel over poorly maintained roads, we are increasing the environmental damage across the country.
There is also an international dimension to the dilemma. Canada and the United States have signed treaties regarding the maintenance of the water quality of the Great Lakes and other waterways. The deterioration of our infrastructure and our incapacity to treat sewage might affect our ability to meet these international environmental obligations.
Obviously any attention to address and halt the damage being done to our environment on a daily basis must include provisions to upgrade and enhance our infrastructure. If we are to turn to the economic aspect of
Supply
municipal infrastructure, and if we are to survive in an increasingly challenging market-place of the next decade and the next century-and I must say that we should be trying not only to survive as a nation but to succeed-it is vital that we become more productive and more efficient as well.
I do not have to spend much time telling members in this House what changing markets and increased competition are costing our regions dependent upon the fisheries, the forests, and/or the steel industry.
If we want to ensure that Canadians, no matter where they live in this country, maintain a certain standard of living and opportunity for employment, we will have to adapt and attract an increasingly selective private sector, but we know already this is not happening.
The hearings we held in large and small municipalities across Canada revealed that opportunities are being lost due to inadequate roads, poor industrial infrastructure, and a lack of services for residential areas. If there are no roads to get workers to the factories, it follows that there will be no factories and no jobs for communities that are searching for new economic development.
I give the example of the United States which has been playing a leadership role in the field of infrastructure. The United States has already taken action on the problem, largely as a result of a report prepared by the National Council on Public Works. The report, presented to the U.S. Congress in 1988, indicated that inadequate infrastructure decreases productivity because private industry must then use its resources and labour to compensate for non-existent or inadequate public infrastructure.
Basically this means that firms compensate by using more capital and labour to produce the same output. What we must learn and learn quickly is that money spent on building or renewing infrastructure is money well spent. I am sure the government shares our concern that wasting money is no longer an option at any level of government.
Studies show that infrastructure may be the factor responsible for a community's demise, or it may be the very element that revitalizes that community. Money spent on municipal infrastructure brings with it a multiplier effect. It results in increased economic activity and higher levels of employment and returns revenues to all

May 25, 1990
Supply
levels of government in the form of direct or indirect taxes and fewer claims on income assistance programs.
In fact a study done by the Federation of Canadian Municipalities in January 1988 showed that a $5 billion investment by each of the municipal, provincial and federal governments would go a long way toward resolving the infrastructure crisis and would create 314,000 jobs. The study estimated that the net cost to the federal government at approximately $416 million was a cost largely due to high interest rates.
It makes sense because not only would municipal infrastructure work be done by Canadians, but the bulk of the required materials could be produced in Canada. These are the short-term benefits. In the long-term Canada's infrastructure, now healthy and expanded to meet the needs of a growing diversified economy, would provide the jobs, homes, and standard of living Canadians have come to expect and deserve no matter where they live.
As well, the various levels of government would benefit from the increased economic base and the decreased number of citizens depending upon government assistance and the advantage of having a modern, competitive workforce and business sector.
Let us turn to the other compelling reason the federal government should become a partner at the municipal and provincial levels. The government has repeatedly refused to help in telling the municipalities that they should increase their water rates to cover the costs of repairing infrastructure such as sewers and roads. Unfortunately, while in need of revision water rates alone are not going to resolve the problem.
Transportation experts in the FCM have also called on the federal government to use some of its revenues collected through taxes on gasoline and fuels to upgrade our neglected roads system. Once again, this only makes sense, yet the federal government refuses to accept its fair share of the responsibility for maintaining and expanding municipal infrastructure. The hardest part of it all is that in the mid-1980s the federal government was a major contributor to the enhancement of the Regina drinking water supply system.
Right now, the government is involved in a multimillion dollar project in Halifax to install sewage treatment facilities. As well, the federal government made a major
commitment during the 1988 election to take part in the clean-up of the St. Lawrence River, which in my view are commendable initiatives. The federal government has to be committed to those initiatives. We have to carry on and meet the rest of the commitment.
Time might be bad. Perhaps the government thinks that with the serious situation facing Canada the infrastructure problem is a temporary one which it will go away. If we listen to the mayors, the reeves, or the natives across our country we learn quickly that this crisis will require the co-operation of all levels of government: everybody. We are all responsible without exception.
By resuming its traditional role with the provincial and municipal governments, the federal government can ensure that no matter where we live in Canada we will have access to clean water and safe roads.
In summary, if we look at municipal infrastructure as a local, isolated problem which each municipal government must handle alone, we have failed to see the bigger picture.

Madam Speaker, I was most interested in the hon. member's comments with respect to the concerns he voiced about developers having a difficult time in providing affordable housing because of the lack of municipal infrastructure.
Also, he made comments with respect to the concerns that the road systems for commuting to the factories and the workplaces were not there, were in bad shape, or potentially would be getting into better shape.
Certainly I am well aware of that and everyone in this country is well aware of that. We are also aware, as are the developers and the hon. member, of the financial difficulties facing the country at the moment and the fact that Canadians are not interested in seeing their taxes raised. They are interested in seeing expenditures cut.
In the discussions of the task force, I wonder if the hon. member and other members of the task force investigated the situation of using the existing infrastructure more intensively, which is not all that bad a condition in most cases.
In fact, Madam Speaker, as you and I are aware there used to be a time when every house in this country had at least five people in it. Today, there is more like two or

three people in it. The infrastructure that was built, that is the roads, the sewers, the schools and the public transportation systems, was to accommodate five or more people in a house are now accommodating only two or three people in a house. The infrastructure is there to accommodate a much greater number of people if there was an intensification of the use of the available land resources.
This is something that lies within the control of municipalities. I hope the hon. member pointed it out to the municipalities and developers. The developers are well aware of the fact and are looking forward to the opportunity to use the existing infrastructure more intensively. I hope that the hon. member, in his task force, pointed that out to the municipalities. I would urge him, if he did not, to urge the municipalities, as he has said, to co-operate with other levels of the government, use the tools at their command to be helpful to solve this problem rather than just looking to the taxpayers of Canada for more and more money.

That is the most interesting comment I have heard in a long time. We are dealing with areas where they do not have infrastructure. I do not understand how the minister wants me to tell a place like Halifax or like St. John's, Newfoundland to use the existing infrastructure for sewage when the only infrastructure they have to put their sewage in is the ocean. There is no infrastructure. There are no treatment facilities. There is no sewage system in place, period.
We are also talking about towns where roads are almost non-existent. We are not dealing with municipalities or with towns where there are existing infrastructures and we can go to those towns and ask them to use those existing facilities.
The FCM report dealt with all those issues.

Madam Speaker, he is talking about the FCM. I would suggest that the hon. minister should make a trip to Atlantic Canada. Perhaps he should go to Fredericton, Sydney in Nova Scotia, and St. John's, Newfoundland. He should go to those different parts of Canada and to the Northwest Territories and have a look at the infrastructure and come back to this House and

stand up without blushing and tell the members of this House that they do have infrastructure.
What I saw across Canada, in the Atlantic as well as in western Canada is unbelievable. In this day and age in a society like the one we live in, still we do not enjoy the proper quality of water that we should be enjoying. We still do not have access to the kind of facilities we need. We still do not have infrastructure in places where we talk about protecting the environment and taking a leadership role on the environmental aspect. Yet we pollute. We are great polluters in western Canada and also in Atlantic Canada and it is our responsibility as a federal government to step in right now and help them out.
There is raw sewage being dumped into the oceans because there are no facilities.

Madam Speaker, it is easy to be critical of the government and I am prepared to do that, but one really has to question the credibility of the Liberal Party on this particular issue since in their years in government they were the ones that began the cut-back on this particular program of the federal involvement with the municipalities. In March 1984 they cut it out completely.

So this task force that the Liberals enacted was an act of hypocrisy, extremely cynical and I would ask the member to defend what he was doing with this task force.
I am amazed, but then again when the criticism comes from colleagues to the left, we sort of understand that it is a sunny day outside and I guess that-
He is light-headed.

The hon. member forgets that the vast majority, if not every program that we have enjoyed up until 1984 was a program that was put in place by a federal Liberal government.
I am amazed that the hon. member would stand up when I already have over 18 pages prepared which specifically outline that it is time for us as federal politicians to stop arguing with one another, face the reality, acknowledge that there is a problem, stop passing

the blame and let us do something constructive for our country and our land.
In this House there are approximately 60 former municipal politicians, whether they were aldermen or mayors. I would ask every one of them to stand up in this House and tell me that while he or she was a mayor or alderman he or she did not promise people to act on issues of that magnitude, did not promise the town or municipality to stand up and defend infrastructure and the needs of the constituency.
We all brag about the environment. We all go back to our constituencies and talk about protecting the environment. Yet we are contributing to the pollution of our beaches and our rivers by not acting now. We are guilty by association. We are guilty by not acknowledging the problem and acting on it.
The hon. member knows, and I have a lot of respect for him, that it is time for action. We have to stop bragging and stop passing on the blame to different people. We have to act now.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Minister of State (Transport)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in today's debate on municipal infrastructure, on behalf of the government and on my own behalf. I believe a number of members in the House this morning are familiar with my own involvement in
May 25, 1990

this question. For 16 years, prior to my election to the House of Commons in November 1988,1 was mayor of a municipality in the Montreal area, and I also took a very active part in the proceedings of the Canadian Federation of Municipalities, both as a member of the board and as President of the Federation. The subject is therefore one that has interested me for some time. Like many members in this House, the subject is of particular interest to me because Canadians live in the towns and villages of this country. All members of this House live in urban or rural communities, with or without infrastructures.
I would like to point out for the benefit of all members that it is not enough to observe that a problem exists and then ask the federal government to take the responsibility for that problem, without considering other circumstances that exist as well.
I think we should realize that the first problem we face in this respect, although not the most serious one, is a very real problem: the jurisdiction of municipal matters lies with the provinces. That is something the federal government must bear in mind. In all negotiations that have taken place over the years on the issue of municipal infrastructure, the provincial governments had to be involved. Today, I can say we have never seen provincial governments rushing to get involved in an issue that by its very nature is first of all a matter of local jurisdiction.
Between 1960 and 1980, the government at the time had gotten into the habit of playing Santa Claus right and left in order to be re-elected, something it managed very successfully for a number of years.

Unfortunately for us and our children, during that 20 year period while the Liberal government of the day was trying to play Santa Claus to everybody, this country accumulated a national debt that is now at the $350 billion level.
In 1984 when this government took office, the annual operating deficit of the government of the day was $16 billion. In other words, the government of the day could not meet its operating expenses. It had to borrow $16 billion a year just to pay the grocery bills.

In the current year, this government, through serious administration and by making difficult decisions, unpopular decisions we all agree, had the courage of assuming our responsibility and-
And doubling the debt.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Minister of State (Transport)
speechtext:
We had to double the debt that was left to us by the previous government, because unfortunately we have to pay the interest on the loan that was accumulated at the time, and 80 per cent of the additional deficit between 1984 and now is due to the deficit that was left to us by the previous government.
From an operating deficit of $16 billion in 1984, this government, through very unpopular decisions that had to be taken for the best interests of Canadians, has turned the situation around. In the current year, we have now an operating surplus of $9 billion. This means a turnaround of $25 billion in a short period of six years.
This is very well explained by the fact that while they were in power, the expenses of the previous government increased every year by 13.9 per cent. This may sound incredible to the Canadian population watching us today on television. But yes, that government had the nerve to increase its expenses by 13.9 per cent every year, accumulating a deficit that we have been paying since taking office, again through unpopular measures that had to be taken in the best interests of Canadians, and our children and grandchildren.
This government reduced the rate of additional expenses every year. It is now 3.5 per cent compared to the 13.9 per cent that we experienced during the term of the Liberal Party.
Therefore, having decided that we would attack the deficit which is the number one priority, it is no surprise that we had to determine that we were going to assume the expenses of our jurisdictions.
And do nothing else.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Minister of State (Transport)

If we do nothing else than bring back the finances of the country to a profitable level where Canadians will be able to compete with the rest of the world and will attain a competitive level where we can bring back prosperity to the country, I think that the present generation and future generations will be forever thankful to this government.

Madam Speaker, in 1980, the previous government, which had been accumulating this kind of increases to the tune of 13.9 per cent annually, decided it was time to do something, and it terminated a program it had established in 1960 because, I assume, it realized that this was not the right way to go about it. So it terminated the program that existed at that time. Obviously, four years later when this government took over the reins of power, we were not about to resume spending in an area that clearly did not lie within our jurisdiction.
We acted responsibly, as the federal authority, by cutting spending and introducing measures that were not popular, because we felt responsible to the citizens of this country.
Earlier, Madam Speaker, I was astonished to hear the first speaker introduce an element in this debate that municipalities have not even had on their shopping list for the past few years, and that is responsibility installing new infrastructures. The whole infrastructure dossier prepared by the Canadian Federation of Municipalities has always focussed on repairs and upgrading of municipal infrastuctures. I am surprised the previous speaker decided to break new ground in an area that is even further removed from the federal government's jurisdiction.
Madam Speaker, if our sole concern was to be popular and to get re-elected, we could keep saying yes to all demands, including some very legitimate ones, that are not our jurisdiction, just to please Canadians for a time. However, I do not think this is what a responsible government should do. A responsible government should, especially in times as difficult as these, be concerned about reducing a monstrous deficit that might otherwise put Canada in a situation that would be unacceptable to our children and our great-grandchildren.
The figures I mentioned earlier, Madam Speaker, and there are any number of statistics on the subject, showed that we are past the stage where we could spend, spend, spend, and hang the consequences. The present deficit, our national debt of $350 billion, is costing this country $40 billion annually in interest alone, nearly one-third of the federal budget.
We are now in a period of budgetary restraint which again forces us to make difficult choices to ensure this country's prosperity. We realize that municipalities, provinces, towns, school boards in fact, everyone has problems. The fact is that in this country, each level of government has specific responsibilities, and each level of government is responsible for deciding where it wants to spend its money. When we look at the budgets and financial situations of the provinces in this country, it is clear that financially, each of these governments is in a far more enviable position than this government, and therefore they are in a position to discharge their responsibilities with respect to municipal jurisdictions and to share these with the municipalities which are also in a pretty healthy financial position.
We are not ignoring a dossier that over the years has been built up by the Canadian Federation of Municipalities and which has shown there are specific problems across the country. However, with my experience of this dossier, I can say that there are considerable differences of opinion between the various municipalities on the way a program should be defined. There are wide differences of opinion between the provinces because in some regions of this country, in some cities and some provinces, the strategy used over the years has allowed them-those cities and provinces-to spend more money on renewing their infrastructure, and now, they are not very pleased with the prospect that other cities and provinces that did not apply this strategy will now enjoy the government's largesse.
Madam Speaker, I think everyone in this country realizes that we have a situation that bears looking into, but the bottom line-

The bottom line is that the federal government has to attack its deficit. That is its number one priority. Once the deficit has been taken care of, then the federal government can look at other ways of spending the taxpayers' money.

Madam Speaker, I am slightly shocked and very surprised. I know the member across the way well, but I forget the name of his riding in the Montreal area. He and I both sat on the board of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities. I recall those days when he was the one who was here meeting with the federal government and trying to dredge more money out of it because of the seriousness of the situation of

infrastructure right across the country. Now, because the member is on the government side of the House, we are hearing a different story. I find that absolutely appalling.
I would like to quote from the remarks of the present President of the FCM at a meeting in Edmonton in February, 1989, where he stated:
And during the 1988 election campaign, a major commitment was made to clean up 1he St. Lawrence River, a commitment which can only be met if significant funds are made available for the improvement and installation of sewage treatment facilities throughout 1he St. Lawrence Valley.
Thus, on the national platform, the government has maintained only opposition to our suggestions while in the context of regional announcements, it has committed to substantial and useful contributions as I have just outlined-A healthy beginning in the infrastructure dialogue would be for the federal government to acknowledge that it is already a financial contributor to Canada's municipal needs, and will undoubtedly continue to be so-
But why does it have to do it on an ad hoc basis? I would like the member to respond to that.

If we do not do so, there will not be a Canada at the turn of the century.

Madam Speaker, I come from an area that is one of the fastest growing areas in Canada and that is Surrey North.
We are in severe trouble because of the lack of municipal infrastructure. We have 9,000 children in portable schools. We do not have money to develop adequate sewers, roads, sidewalks, parks, and recreation facilities. We have had to send out notices to parents to say that they cannot put their children into minor league ball, sports, and athletic activities because we do not have a base to raise the dollars to put in those types of services. There have been discussions that we are $282 million behind our ability to meet the basic infrastructure necessary for a viable community.
Our community has very little industry and commerce. It is a residential community. It does not have the tax base.
Why does the hon. member feel that the federal government has no responsibility to those types of communities and the families in those communities?
Second, if the government is so worried about the deficit, why did it allow the interest rates to go up yesterday to over 14 per cent?

Madam Speaker, I think the hon. member will certainly agree with me that the responsibility of all elected people at all levels is to manage the local affairs and assume the responsibilities for the decisions that are taken for the local authorities.
I repeat that this government has a national debt of $350 billion. It is costing Canadian taxpayers $40 billion annually in interest payments alone. The priority of the government is to look after that deficit within its own jurisdiction before looking at other problems in other jurisdictions because, if we do not attack the problem of that deficit, there will not be a Canada in a few years and we will not have the money to do anything which is under our direct jurisdiction.

repairs, infrastructures, local responsibility-

If that is the case, I refer to the Ottawa-Carleton area where there is over $1 billion in repairs going on. The basic theme of your government is "user pay". The taxpayers of this area are paying. The individual taxpayers are paying. The merchant taxpayers are paying. The industrial taxpayers are paying. But there is one freeloader, and you are the one who is freeloading. You are not paying your fair share.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. member will want to continue after Question Period.

It being eleven o'clock, pursuant to Standing Order 30(5), the House will now proceed to Members' Statements pursuant to Standing Order 31.

Madam Speaker, I am proud to announce in the House today an environmental initiative launched by a family in my riding of London-Middlesex.
Called "A Human Race Towards A Healthy Planet", the Stephens family has launched a trans-Canada bicycle expedition to raise environmental awareness and to encourage students and families world-wide to adopt positive action and attitude towards a healthy planet.
David and Andrew Stephens are doing the cycling with the rest of the family in support. They started out on May 1 from Victoria, B.C. and this Sunday they will be in my riding of London-Middlesex on their way to St. John's, Newfoundland for Canada's birthday, July 1.
David Stephens is a young Canadian who believes that actions speak louder than words. His actions tell all of us that a healthy planet starts with one person's commitment to make a difference.
The Stephens' human race towards a healthy planet shows how one family, when committed to a cause and working together, can make a difference. Their focus is on working together for a positive cause. Their example to the families of Canada is simple; let's work together to make one healthy, happy country from sea to sea. We should congratulate their efforts.

Madam Speaker, "Please extend your hands and hearts toward Lithuania", plead the President of the Lithuanian Medical Association and the Minister of Health as they call for urgent medical assistance.
The economic blockade imposed by Moscow on Lithuania has severed basic medical services and supplies to that republic. Doctors are concentrating on emergency cases only and stocks of essential medications and surgical supplies, such as insulin, antibiotics, gloves, and intravenous sets, are being critically depleted.
The health minister has predicted that the rate of infectious diseases would increase, performance of essential surgical operations would be hindered and deaths otherwise preventable would become an eventuality.
I urge this government to respond to the plea of Lithuanians, to bring their cause to the attention of President Gorbachev when he and our Prime Minister meet next week, and to obtain Mr. Gorbachev's commitment that he will ensure the medical safety of every Lithuanian man, woman and child. We have faith in Mr. Gorbachev and therefore trust in his continuing good will.

Madam Speaker, in 1976 I first raised the issue of the impact of industrial pollution on the respiratory systems of Canadians. For a number of years I argued that sulphur dioxide emissions were directly related to the higher
May 25, 1990

than normal rate of respiratory infections and lung cancers in the residents of Thunder Bay.
Today, 14 years later, a study conducted by 11 Canadian and American Lung Association scientists clearly states that acid air can damage human lungs as badly as acid rain damages forests, lakes and trees. It also states that acid aerosols are increasing bronchitis, asthma and deaths from respiratory failure.
The federal and provincial governments should act immediately on this very serious matter. They should act by establishing monitoring devices and reporting daily to the residents of smokestack communities. They should work harder to eliminate the pollutants themselves, and they should continue to conduct studies to ensure that we have a full understanding of the impact of this chemical on the well-being of Canadians.

Madam Speaker, up until a few days ago, the people in my riding could not take the current constitutional question too seriously. However, recent developments have brought this situation to the forefront of every conversation.
Still the question often is, why does Quebec want so much? The answer is simple, they do not.
Since arriving here 18 months ago, I have gotten to know Quebecers for the very first time. The Quebec members that I now know are teachers and business people, mayors and journalists, mechanics, engineers, doctors and pharmacists, just like home. All they really want is to keep their way of life and culture, just as we in Atlantic Canada want to keep our unique culture.
There is a great deal of concern and speculation throughout the country about our future, and it is up to all parliamentarians, legislators and our leaders to bring this country together, because if we do not, none of us will be able to keep our way of life and all of our unique cultures in Canada.

Madam Speaker, I wish to alert the House to the serious potential danger to international peace and security posed by the current
escalation in the dispute between India and Pakistan over the status of Kashmir.
This dispute has existed since India and Pakistan became independent in 1947. The two countries have fought a war over the region twice, in 1948 and again in 1965. Hundreds of people, including many civilians, have been killed in recent clashes that threaten to erupt into a third war.
In 1948 Canada, as a member of the United Nations Security Council, was instrumental in stopping the war between India and Pakistan over Kashmir.
It is time for Canada to act again. We should use our current place in the Security Council to increase international pressure on the two sides to affirm their commitment to the 1965 ceasefire, withdraw military forces from the ceasefire line, desist from indiscriminate violence against civilians and negotiate peaceful solutions to the conflict. Canada should encourage the UN Secretary General to offer his good offices to achieve a just and lasting settlement. The international community should act now before it is too late.

Madam Speaker, in the fall in 1959 I left my home in Alberta to study at a university in Montana. While attending Montana State University, I became familiar with the frequent discussions about a proposed amendment to the American Constitution.
Today, as I address this House, the American public is again engaged in yet another consideration for a constitutional amendment to their Constitution. Since the Constitution of the United States was ratified in 1787, there has been a total of 26 amendments.
Clearly, what some Canadian premiers must come to understand is that it is not a requirement for Canada to construct a constitution that resolves all issues in all situations for all time at one moment. What is required is the building of an agreement by which the procedures for change are known and agreed upon. Thereafter, the first ministers will be able to meet the challenges of an unforeseen future.
Had the Fathers of Confederation applied the standards of perfection that are being imposed by some

May 25, 1990
premiers today, the British North America Act of 1867 never could have been written. What is required now-

Madam Speaker, I rise today on an extremely serious matter, that is the escalation of tensions in the truckers' blockade.
Contrary to news reports this morning, the truckers have not left their blockade, quite simply because they do not believe this government when it says it will review their concerns. Indeed, I have just received a call from the president of a trucking firm who said that when one of his rigs tried to pull out of the line-up this morning, the driver was threatened by a shotgun-toting individual and told to pull back in the line or else. This incident occurred only a few hours ago at a Quebec border crossing.
The time to address the issues which have caused this blockade is now. This government has procrastinated and failed to acknowledge the inequities between the Canadian and American truckers until there were blockades set up at border crossings throughout eastern Canada.
I implore this government to take action today to resolve these inequities. I would certainly hope that we do not have to wait until there is further escalation, violence and even injury, before this government acts to ensure the competitiveness of the essential Canadian trucking industry.

Madam Speaker, Mr. Pocklington said last night, "Alberta demands champions". The Wetaskiwin Relics recently won a COHA World Cup tournament in San Diego. Now, for the fifth time in seven years, the Edmonton Oilers have won the Stanley Cup.
Hear, hear.

I was going to ask the House to join me in congratulating the management, Mr. Sather, Mr. Pocklington and others such as the coaching staff of Messrs. Muckier, Green and Low, and in particular, all the families and players of the Oilers hockey club for their victory. Congratulations as well to Mr. Bill Ranford in winning the Conn Smythe Trophy.
Once again it shows all Canadians across the country that if you set your goals high and believe in yourself, you can accomplish and succeed in anything you do.

Madam Speaker, Eurasian milfoil, an aquatic weed that has choked many of the lakes and rivers in the B.C. interior has defeated all efforts to control its spread.
Mechanical harvesting, while able to slow the growth of the weed, is unable to eradicate it. The weed is affecting the recreational and tourism potential of B.C.'s interior lakes.
Municipal and provincial governments have called for federal assistance to control this aquatic weed. It is therefore most disappointing to learn that Eurasian milfoil is not being researched for biological control by Agriculture Canada.
The Okanagan Basin Water Board has appealed to the Minister of Agriculture to get directly involved in developing the long-term biological controls necessary to preserve the resource value of the Okanagan Valley. Nothing has been done.
It is absolutely essential that the Minister of Agriculture make a strong commitment to research ways of eradicating Eurasian milfoil before the environmental impact of its uncontrolled growth gets completely out of hand.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Loran-C is a very reasonably priced, helpful aid for private pilots in Canada. It is an aid to navigation that provides distance measuring equipment, indications of speed, headings and also information on airports in a region where a person is flying.
May 25, 1990

At the moment, Loran-C is available to the maritime regions of Canada and to parts of Quebec and Ontario, but it is not available with any degree of accuracy on the prairies.
I would encourage the Minister of Transport to take a very close look at Loran-C and provide an option of having this navigation system available to private and general aviation pilots throughout the prairie regions. It provides safety, a large degree of accuracy and would be very much appreciated by the private pilots of Canada.

Madam Speaker, it is becoming increasingly urgent for the First Ministers of Canada to find an acceptable and equitable solution to the current constitutional impasse. We are witnessing daily reports in the media on this issue which could have very serious consequences for the country.
The Meech Lake debate has caused a number of unfortunate events to occur throughout the country that do not reflect the wishes of a majority of Canadians who desire to have a united Canada.
We live in a great country built on the efforts of two founding peoples, and with the contribution made by people who came to Canada from other lands. Some of these people knew firsthand the terrible face of internal strife, political instability and economic chaos. Together with English and French speaking Canadians, and with the aboriginal peoples of Canada who recognized the beauty and potential of the land, we have built a country which we are all proud to call home.
We are indeed fortunate, and we all have an interest in working towards a better tomorrow for our country and for our children.

Madam Speaker, today Albertans are proud to salute our Premier Don Getty for his leadership in support of the Meech Lake Accord.
Premier Getty's constructive proposal to pass Meech Lake now and adopt a list of principles to be discussed during a set period of time is a constructive proposal.
As the Prime Minister said yesterday: "Don Getty put the signature of the Government of Alberta on a piece of paper which was designed in Alberta's interest, in the interests of western Canada and, most of all, in the interests of a united Canada."
Premier Getty said: "I propose to honour the accord because it is indispensable that we all do so in the interests of Canadian unity."

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canada Post is at it again. This time the victim is the Vars post office in my riding.
Last fall, residents of Vars heard a rumour and reacted swiftly by signing a petition against the closure of their post office. Some 374 residents, more than half of the community, signed the petition which I tabled in this House on December 8, 1989.
Vars is a growing community and even Canada Post admits as much. Yet the residents of Vars have just been "consulted" and their post office will be closing this summer.
These closures of post offices against the will of the people are done in the name of expenditure reduction, even if an outlet is profitable.
On behalf of the residents of Vars, I urge the minister to tell us today that he will instruct his officials to keep the Vars post office open.

Madam Speaker, the housing crisis in Canada continues to worsen. The Canadian Homebuilders' Association has documented that, because of high interest rates, half the first-time home buyers have been forced out of the market. Residential construction activity in the first four months of 1990 is down. In April, the applications for residential building permits decreased.
What is the government's response to the growing crisis in housing? The Minister of State for Housing has told the mayor of Vancouver that he has no funds available to assist in developing affordable housing. Now

May 25, 1990
Oral Questions
the government has dealt another blow by increasing the bank rate to over 14 per cent. This can only have a devastating effect on an already bleak housing market. It appears that this government wishes not only to bring the housing industry to its knees, but it wishes to knock it flat on its back.

Madam Speaker, I rise today on behalf of my constituents of Halifax who are fearful. Haligonians, indeed all Nova Scotians, are fiercely devoted to Canada. From its founding in 1749 through pre-Confederation battles, the birth of our nation in 1867, two World Wars, and up to the present, the Warden of the North and its people have believed steadfastly in this country and its future.
To us a Canada without the francophone fact, without Quebec, is unthinkable. We have so little time but we must ensure that Canada, worth so much, is not allowed to wither.

We have 29 days left to resolve the constitutional impasse. We must find solutions for our own benefit but also for our children, who have a right to inherit this beautiful, vast country of ours that is Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Transport.
The blockage of border crossings this week by hundreds of angry Canadian truckers has brought home to Canadians just how important the trucking industry is for our economy. It has also brought home to Canadians just how harmful and ill considered it was for this government to put into effect full deregulation of the trucking industry without first being sure that American truckers have to live by the same rules of this country as Canadians. In fact thousands of jobs have been lost in
Ontario in the trucking industry since this deregulation went into effect. I understand that the blockages have eased at certain border points like Windsor but are continuing at other border points.
One of the issues of concern to Canadian truckers is the issue of cabotage, the picking up and unloading of cargoes within Canada by Americans. Has the government begun enforcing our already existing laws against cabotage and, if not, could the minister tell us exactly when the government will begin enforcing these laws to resolve this ongoing issue, which is of great concern to Canadian truckers in terms of their jobs and their industry?

Madam Speaker, I appreciate my hon. friend's question.
No one is at issue with the fact that trucking is important to Canada. That is the reason I went to Windsor on Wednesday night-Thursday morning to meet with representatives of the independent truckers in an effort, with the assistance of the Minister of Transport of Ontario, to alleviate the situation.
As far as the issue of cabotage is concerned, we discussed that with the independent truckers. There are methods in place at the present time to make sure that it does not happen. It is a combination of an effort by Minister of Employment and Immigration and by the Minister of National Revenue. We had discussions with the provincial officials, and we have agreed to work together to see if we can improve methods of detecting cabotage, where it is occurring. Those discussions are ongoing.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canadians will find it strange that the minister is unable to tell us that he and the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Minister of National Revenue are enforcing laws that are already on the books. It would be reassuring if he could tell us that that enforcement by his own colleagues and himself is beginning this weekend.
Madam Speaker, my second question is directed to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
May 25, 1990

It is particularly disturbing to see that some trucking companies in the United States are applying allegedly aggressive and unfair pricing policies that are prejudicial to Canadian truckers.
Has the Bureau of Competition Policy started to investigate these practices, and if not, when will it do so? This is another matter that is important to the trucking industry in this country, an industry that is in turn very important to our economy.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think we must realize that the Bureau of Competition Policy has a job to do and that it is in a position to respond to complaints that are filed with the Bureau.
However, it is not particularly easy when the hon. Leader of the Opposition starts accusing everyone by saying there are problems with the Bureau of Competition Policy, without being specific.
My colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, whom I am representing today and I, as Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, are here, and we have legislation and regulations to deal with this. However, any serious complaints must first be identified and individuals and companies named, and only then will we be able to act.
I can assure you that we have all the resources we need to act, but I think the Leader of the Opposition should act responsibly and specify the nature of his charges so that we can do something about them.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is up to the minister to listen to Canadian truckers, and he should not avoid doing so when they have complaints to make. I hope he will listen to those complaints and act on them.
Finally, Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of National Revenue.

I want to know if the Minister of National Revenue has begun collecting the federal excise tax on gasoline to the same extent as the burden of that tax is imposed on Canadian truckers. If not, I would like him to tell us exactly when he will begin doing so.

Madam Speaker, it appears at the present time-and this comes forward from previous administrations, so I have no
Oral Questions
embarrassment in saying it-that there is no effective measure for collecting federal excise tax on shall we say full tanks of gas coming from the United States, whether it is in a Canadian truck or an American truck.
We discussed the method of the Ontario government of trying to collect its Ontario sales tax on the fuel. We undertook-and are moving on it immediately-to look at some method whereby we in Canada could begin to collect tax on full tanks of fuel in an effort to level out the playing field.
Ontario agreed to work with us on this initiative, and we will report back when we have something that we can deal with. I would hope at that time, if it requires legislation, that my hon. friend, the Leader of the Opposition, would ensure the House on behalf of his party speedy co-operation and no delays in the Senate.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
Yesterday the Minister of Finance lectured the House that high interest rates were necessary in order to keep Canadian costs of doing business competitive.
Also, yesterday the finance committee heard from Mr. James Taylor, President of the Canadian Exporters Association, who said: "the government's"-that is the Tory government-"high interest rate and high dollar policies are equal to a self-imposed tariff of 10 per cent on Canadian exports to the U.S. and 15 per cent on Canadian products sold overseas".
When is the government going to abandon this high interest, high dollar rate and allow Canadian exporters to be competitive on world markets and save Canadian jobs which have been going down-71,000 in the first four months of this year?

Madam Speaker, I think the hon. member will see, if he reviews the export figures over the last seven, eight or nine months, a gradual increasing trend in our export performance. While I accept the fact that the export sector of our economy is under pressure because of the interest rate policy that we are following, the same sector has been able to demonstrate increasing competitiveness and therefore an ability still to tap into foreign markets in spite of this policy.

May 25, 1990
Oral Questions
I say to my hon. friend and I say to Mr. Thylor of the export association, as I have said to him on a number of occasions: if we do not deal with these underlying threats to our competitive position, the ongoing impact on individual companies in the export sector will be permanent.
It is important that we preserve this competitive position, and that means getting the inflationary pressures down. I remind my hon. friend that in 1989 we started the year with a 4.5 per cent increase in unit labour costs. That is the best measure of our competitive position that I can give. We started at 4.5 per cent and by the end of the year it was 6.9 per cent. That says we are losing business. If we continue that way we will lose business on a permanent basis, and that lost business means lost jobs.
Because of your policies.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
I have a supplementary question for the same minister, Madam Speaker.
The minister must admit that his policies are not working. Will he finally tell the House that his budget of last February does not help Canadians, does not help Canadian exports and that it is destroying the Canadian economy? Will he give us a new budget as soon as possible to correct the economic situation the country is in?

Madam Speaker, my colleague has just referred to the difficulties with the budget. I would ask him to address his colleagues in the Senate because there are two bills right now that are being held up by the Senate.
They are being studied.
Have a conference.

The exclusive difference between the House of Commons and the Senate is on these bills. The questions are who decides to raise taxes and where should the spending cuts be?
If the Senate persists in doing this, what it is providing is a loan to the large corporations in this country which is in the hundreds of millions of dollars now. I have heard my colleagues opposite ask: "Why do you not you ensure that the tax system is fair and that large corporations are properly taxed?" Today, large corporations are not paying a large corporations tax simply because the bill has not been passed by the Senate. Until the Senate-
And they will not after.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Essex-Windsor.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Transport who has himself created much of the problem that has existed in central Canada this week among the truckers. The fact is that the minister was requested at least a month ago-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Who made the request?

-to have a meeting with the key parties which have been involved in this protest. There was no response to that request.
Now another telegram has come from some of the same parties: the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway and Transport Workers, the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, the Transportation and Communications International Union. They have asked this minister if he is prepared to have an urgent meeting with them to discuss these problems that exist across the province, problems that persist today.
The minister knows himself that the blockade at Fort Erie is still in place. He knows that truckers across the province-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member does have a question.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, no, it is a major speech.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Twenty minutes, Madam Speaker.

My question is the following: In view of the continuing reality of these trucking blockades, is the minister prepared to meet with the groups that told him
May 25, 1990

by telegram that they need an urgent meeting to discuss the crisis they see for truckers in central Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Questions and comments on the member's speech.

Madam Speaker, that was a great question on Tuesday and Wednesday, but it is a little late on Friday.
1 was asked to go down to Windsor. I did go down on Wednesday night after the vote. I met with representatives of the independent truckers, and I guess that is key. There was no association there in terms of an elected representative or president, et cetera. That is part of the difficulty.
I met with representatives from those involved in the blockade on Thursday morning. We discussed their concerns. We agreed that we could satisfy their concerns.
We came out of the meeting and had a public meeting with the media. They were satisfied, the words were: "David's won". Unfortunately, David could not go back to the blockade and deliver all the other Davids. So we do not have the blockade lifted.
I regret that as much as you do. I made copies of my letter available to everybody. We are prepared to do what we can.
We have had the meeting you asked for. It just has not had the results we all want.

Madam Speaker, I wrote to the minister on April 17 on behalf of these various unions requesting an urgent meeting because of these problems. The minister has not responded to that request. He has attempted to say that there are no problems that existed in the industry.
Is the minister prepared to respond to this telegram that has now reached him, a telegram which comes not from the independent truckers but from the many employees of trucking firms across this province? They are the key people at this stage who are carrying forward this trucking blockade. Is he prepared to meet and take some serious action?

Madam Speaker, I am prepared to respond to any request once I
Oral Questions
get it. To the best of my knowledge, it has not been received by my department. It has been delivered to my hon. friend. That is fair ball.
I understand that he is going to be dealing with his colleagues in the various unions. I do not knock that. If they want to meet and have discussions with me, they would be better off doing it directly rather than delaying it by going through my friend.

Madam Speaker, I have to say to the minister that this is not a telegram to me. This is a telegram to him, a copy of which I happen to have. If he has not seen it, it is his department's fault, not my fault.
I want to ask my supplementary question of the Minister of Employment and Immigration since the Minister of Employment Immigration has also had a suggestion from the ministry in Ontario to the effect that people be deputized in the Ontario Department of Transport to enforce the immigration laws of this country against U.S. truckers who are taking loads from places that they are not supposed to.
Is the minister prepared to make a commitment at this stage that in fact she will accept this quite legitimate, straightforward and sensible suggestion from the ministry in the province of Ontario that this deputization of the transport ministry officials in Ontario take place? Will she take that advice? Will she act?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, like my other colleagues, I am working very closely with the Minister of Transport on what is a very difficult issue, and one that I think the Minister of Transport has developed a strategy for. He has been very accommodating. I will continue to work with him on this.

Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of the Environment my question is directed to the acting Prime Minister.
Yesterday outside the House the new Minister of the Environment refused to endorse this government's policy to stabilize carbon dioxide emissions by the year 2000.

May 25, 1990
Oral Questions
It is a commitment that was made by his predecessor two weeks ago, and confirmed last week in the House by the Minister of Forestry when he said, as reported at page 11612 of Hansard: "These are federal commitments".
Is it government policy to stabilize carbon dioxide emissions by the year 2000?

Madam Speaker, as you know, the Minister of the Environment is in Winnipeg attending consultation sessions that are being held throughout Canada which will result in the development of commitments to the Green Plan that will be taken to the international conference in Geneva this November.
The minister responded to questions yesterday outside the House which confirmed what his predecessor said in Bergen, namely, that Canada aims at stabilizing CO2 emissions in our country by the year 2000. His leadership was reflected in the Bergen declaration.
The hon. member should know that in order to achieve a target like that it will require sacrifices on the part of every Canadian. In fact it will require changes in our life-styles. This is why we have engaged in such a comprehensive consultation process which will result in the announcement of these commitments that are possible and sustainable later on this year.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister.
The former Minister of the Environment committed this government unconditionally to stabilize carbon dioxide emissions. The Minister of Forestry confirmed this in the House last week.
I want to ask the acting Prime Minister why this government is back-tracking on this very important issue? How does he expect Canadians to believe anything that this government now says about the environment?
Madam Speaker, there is no back-tracking, as the hon. member would know if she had studied the deliberations of the Bergen commission.
The Bergen commission did not make any commitments.

There are those who say that it would actually be possible by the year 2000 to attain a 20 per cent reduction of CO2 emissions, particularly throughout the industrialized world.
The minister has stated on behalf of Canada a Canadian target, a Canadian commitment to stabilize by the year 2000 the greenhouse gases that are emitted in Canada to current 1990 levels. There is no confusion about that.
What we are doing now is consulting with Canadians who would have to accommodate these kinds of commitments. We will be the government by the year 2000. The hon. member will realize then that what we have done and what we have committed to will actually have been achieved.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
He will know that the recent Atlantic fisheries aid package contained nothing, not a single red cent, for inshore fishermen and the related plant workers who are the victims of massive catch failure.
His colleague, the Minister for International Trade, said last week that the government was waiting until the end of the season. If he is talking about the winter season, it ended seven weeks ago. If he is talking about the summer season, it will not end until October. Surely, he is not suggesting that we wait until then.
Is the government now prepared to recognize the desperate plight in which those people find themselves right now? Is the government prepared to act right now to do something to help them ease their pain?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the government recognizes that there are problems in the inshore fishery. Those matters have been considered in companion with other actions taken by the government with regard particularly to problems caused relating to the stocks of northern cod.
I would not want to cause the hon. member to believe that there will be an imminent announcement with regard to the inshore fishery.
May 25, 1990

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same minister.
He will know that 100,000 workers in Atlantic Canada make their living either in the fishing boats or in the fish plants. His colleague, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, admitted a week or so ago that the government has a plan to downsize that number.
Is the minister now in a position to tell us how many fishermen are going to be zapped, if you like, and be wiped out by the government's drive to downsize the fishery? Is he prepared to indicate whether there is a hit list of communities, if you like, that will be wiped off the face of the map by the government's mad scheme?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member and I have had an exchange before about policies designed to end fishing communities in Newfoundland.
Your comments went over like a lead balloon last time, too.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There were policies of that kind brought in by a former Liberal government of Newfoundland. But they are not part of the plans of this government. Nor is any part of the plan of this government, if I may use his moderate language, to zap fishermen or to take any other actions of that kind.
There is a recognition that there is a serious problem in the fishery and, among other things, that there is a need to help prepare people who are in the fishing industry who will not be able to continue to find full lives in that industry, adapt to other opportunities. That was part of the announcement that was made by my colleague the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. That is part of the policy that this government is following.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. It relates to the Meech Lake impasse and the activities that are occurring at this time.
Oral Questions
As the Deputy Prime Minister knows, we are very concerned that the constitutional impasse over the Meech Lake Accord be resolved. But there are other Canadians who are concerned as well-northerners, women, aboriginal Canadians-that they not be left out of the process completely. They are concerned that by the nature of the behind-the-scenes negotiations they will again be left out, that their concerns will not be addressed, that they will not be informed of the nature of the discussions.
What assurances can the Deputy Prime Minister and the Prime Minister give that this will not be a done deal between the Prime Minister and the ten Premiers? What assurances can he give those many, many Canadians who are concerned so that the deal can be done, and that there can be an honest resolve to this impasse?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:

How will it complement the government's other efforts of support for central and east European nations?

Mr. Speaker, I will be representing Canada at the final signing of the agreements bringing into effect the new European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
We will have a participation in this bank of something like 3.4 per cent, which is the eighth-largest participation of the banks.
The initiative is basically a French initiative, but one to which the Prime Minister responded in a very important way because of our commitment to supporting what is happening in eastern Europe. The bank itself will support the reforms that are being undertaken in eastern Europe, in particular the desires of those countries to move into a market-oriented economy with good involvement of the private sector. The activities of the bank will support the private sector. Its mandate is specifically designed to do that.
In addition to that, we will be taking into account the importance of dealing with environmental problems in eastern European countries.
This new bank does complement the support that we have provided to these countries over the past few months. It is a more cost-effective way of providing that support since it is through a bank and therefore can be levered through borrowings by the bank in the financial markets.
In addition to that, we will help provide stronger support for our private sector companies in accessing that market and participating more aggressively in those markets.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I just want to raise a short point of order respecting activities which occurred last night. My point of order concerns a quorum call in the Chamber late last night. Representatives of the parties in this House had worked out, and agreed on, and understood the effect of, the terms of the special order under which debate on the bill was being conducted. These same channels, as we call them, understood that the Chair and its advisers understood and agreed that the terms of the order meant what they said. Debate on the bill would continue until the times set out in the order, or until no further member rose on debate. It would be by vote on the question for third reading, and nothing else, that this stage of the bill would be disposed of.
Much of the understanding by the House seems to have been breached last night when the New Democratic Party proposed a unanimous consent motion right off the wall. There had been no consultation. Then when a quorum count was called, I was surprised that the Chair even entertained, or accepted, either of these proposals. The reason is simply because of the special order, which had been put in place.
Because of that order, members were preparing their remarks for debate or were following debate in places nearby where they could watch the debate through the broadcast system. They were doing this in good faith, based on the all-party special order made by unanimous consent after full consultations.
However, it seems we are faced with a possible new principle given last night's antics. Is it now the case that orders adopted by unanimous consent are binding only on those members who are in the House when the order is made or, even worse, that any member can later change his or her mind and start deviating from or challenging the order?
In conclusion, I think it would best serve the House if the Chair could perhaps, not immediately, report back with a ruling on the weight of a special order in place for this debate. If such orders do not prevent proposals such as made last night, or other proposals from being
received by the Chair, then we had all better know about it now so that in future we can take this into account.
Madam Speaker, we operate on the basis of what has been presumed to be practice. We had operated, not in a vacuum, but based on old advice and word given, and so on. Therefore it was with some surprise we saw that the special order-and there were other unwritten things- was tantamount to Standing Orders that supersede the existing ongoing Standing Orders for the duration of that bill, and only that bill. To find out that is not now the case, as I say, was a bit of a surprise.
I hope the Chair might be able to find some means by which we could establish a modus vivendi that would allow us to operate on the basis that we tried to operate on yesterday and which I think is in everybody's interest, on the government side of the House, the opposition side of the House and, certainly, the Chair. So it is in that context that I ask the Chair to consider this point of order.
You are full of nonsense.

The petitioners call on Parliament to support the maintenance of all postal services from the existing full service post office in the town of Wilkie and to reject any proposals that would result in the closing of the existing post office.
I support the petitioners and call on the government to respond favourably to their pleas.
