May 25, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I commend the Liberals for bringing this very important issue to the floor of the House. That is about the only positive thing I can say about the Liberals at this time as pertains to this particular issue.
Although honourable in some ways, I must suggest that Canadians should be somewhat cynical of their task force simply because the Liberals when in government continually cut back on financial assistance for municipalities. Finally, in March 1984 they terminated it.
One really has to wonder why the Liberals would cross this country asking for input from municipalities when they knew full well what the municipalities were going to say to them. In fact, they had initiated or were a part of the crisis. I think that puts it in an appropriate perspective.
Some of my colleagues indicated to me that it is National Fitness Week. I should have been aware of that, but in particular, it is "sneaker day'' I understand. I caution Canadians that if you are going to put on your sneakers and get out there running, there is a grave danger that you will hurt yourself while running on the sidewalks of this country.
Or disappear into a pot-hole.

Or disappear into a pot-hole. I notice that the ex-mayor of Moncton, now I believe the member, said in 1987 that it would take $3.5 million to bring the sidewalks of Moncton up to par so that people would not get hurt. Not all cities are as fortunate as Ottawa to have running trails.
Last year, I took the opportunity to go out to see Meech Lake. It was a place I had to see, and I am in accord with the agreement. I want to tell you that the roadway that led to Meech Lake was a disaster. Maybe it would be a symbolic gesture if we did something about that roadway on the way to Meech.
As a former municipal politician, I am very pleased to speak because I think the municipal level of government is the most accountable one. It is the one that is the most responsible. It has less bureaucracy for citizens to get involved with. They simply call their alderperson, voice a complaint and I think most of the time these people respond.
Supply
I am going to use my community, and not surprisingly so, as an example of the plight in which municipalities find themselves and have found themselves in for a long time. It is suggested in the community of Sault Ste. Marie that it would take $15 million a year to maintain the status quo on road, sewer and bridge infrastructure in the community. The community can spend only $5 million. You can see that the rate of deterioration will be catastrophic unless addressed. The community is forced, and I am sure all communities are doing this, to restructure priorities. It will have to look after only arterials and collectors. The residential streets will be untouched.
Talking about bridge safety, there are several bridges in the community that have weight limits, that is on a truck route which is completely ironical at best and paradoxical at worst. They are safety hazards. There are hundreds of grade separations in this country where nothing has been done and nothing will be done unless the municipalities and the provinces decide to do something. It is a financial impossibility.
Until 1984 the federal government was involved. In March 1984 the Liberal government said: "We cannot be involved any more. It is too costly." Now the Liberals are saying: "If we were in power, if we were the government of this country, we would be very much involved with the municipal infrastructure."
What do the two upper levels of government say? The provincial government says: "We are on side. We want to participate but we cannot participate unless the the federal government participates." The federal government says: "Constitutionally we cannot involve ourselves. Municipalities are creatures of the provinces not the federal government." Yet the federal government does involve itself when it is appropriate to do so. If the timing is right and if the expediency is right, the government does get involved with municipal infrastructure.
It gets involved in an ad hoc way from here to there across this country but with no national strategy whatsoever. This begs the three levels of government to sit down together and discuss the crisis in this country respecting infrastructure. We cannot say: "It is your problem. It is not my problem."
I think of the people in California saying: "I live in Los Angeles. I know that an earthquake is going to occur, but

May 25, 1990
Supply
I am going to stay anyway and suffer the risk." It is admirable, I suppose courageous, but one really has to wonder. This government is saying it knows there is a crisis, but it cannot address it.
It saddened me to hear the member for Anjou-Ri-viere-des-Prairies, who was a well respected president of FCM, calling local governments Santa Clauses when they are in power. I tell you that that member was the Kris Kringle of FCM. He was there every year, year after year, saying the federal government must involve itself. Why now, when asked a question, does the minister say absolutely nothing? He talks about deficit, he says to the municipalities: "I am sorry, there is nothing further we can do." Pie completely avoids that issue.
On June 4, 1988 he said: "I think there is a thaw coming in Ottawa." Well, I think the thaw has stopped and it is a freeze again. The federal government is not about to get involved. I have clippings from 1985, 1986, 1987 and 1988 saying: "We are willing to listen; we want to talk." Many ministers have spoken. The Deputy Prime Minister said: "I have an answer for you; double your water rates." That will go down well, will it not.
That was the former Minister of the Environment.

Was it? Thank you. Whoever said it, it is sheer folly and the government knows that. It is passing the buck in a sense, but in the other sense, it will not pass the buck because it cut transfer payments. On the one hand it passes the buck but on the other hand, it says it cannot pass the buck because it does not have any bucks to pass. It is obvious hypocrisy.
I do not think the government has to say it is going to address the problem immediately and will get involved in this $15 billion or $16 billion big fix as the FCM calls it, and appropriately so because it has to be a big fix or this country is going to deteriorate. The streets, the sidewalks, the bridges, the very structures below them are crumbling. I think everybody understands that. Remediation and rehabilitation of roadways and bridges will cost one-tenth the cost of redoing the whole project, so money spent now will be money spent, yes. It will cost billions, maybe $15 billion to $20 billion, but if we let it go on it will cost 10 times that much. That is obviously a foolhardy way of dealing with the problem.
The federal government does involve itself with housing programs for municipalities, but do you think that the province and the federal government get together on those programs? Certainly not. They do not overlap. They are not dovetailed. They are separate programs. Why would anybody do that? Could they not get together and say: "We will dedicate this much money. Let us put it together. It makes a lot of sense." But no. Politically they say: "We want to take credit for this program" and the provinces say: "We want to take credit for this program". It begs liaison; it begs co-operation.
A department of municipal affairs does not need to have billions of dollars to start off, but I think it behoves the federal government to initiate discussion among the three levels. If the federal government took the lead and the province implemented or at least directed the program, the municipalities would be able to implement it. They are the people who best can implement the program.
The Minister of Finance had the gall to say: "Whenever we get involved with the municipalities we do not think we get our money's worth". What an appalling statement to make to municipal people. I think what he was saying is that we do not get our political money's worth. Whatever funds municipalities get from whichever level of government always have strings attached. In fact, one might say that they have a very heavy rope attached.
"You can have x thousands of dollars if you spend it this way. We will tell you how to spend your money, we know better than you do". Funds with strings attached is ridiculous. "We will give you 75 per cent if you spend 25 per cent on this project". It is not a way of handling a problem. Sometimes municipalities are duped or forced to get into a situation where they say: "Well, if we do not take the money, it will go elsewhere". This ad hoc treatment is not acceptable to anyone.
Government programs like deregulation which bring larger, longer and heavier trucks into our highway system and without trains only serve to exacerbate the problem. The decimation of VIA Rail puts more heavy buses on the roadway. This only exacerbates the problem. It requires at least a standardized national program among the three levels of government to say: "Here is the problem, how will we address it?"
May 25, 1990

This government is devoid of any creativity. Not one positive step toward addressing this problem has been mentioned. It would not necessarily take a national program immediately. Let us sit down and discuss it. There must be creative ways, such as taking a cent from the gasoline tax and giving it directly to the municipalities commensurate with the amounts of money that they spend in the local municipality. It would be a proportionate division of funds. I am not saying that is an answer. I do not even know how much money that would give to a municipality, but it is just one creative thought.
I know the minister is very sympathetic and a very creative individual. Given the opportunity with the three levels, I know this positive dialogue would address the situation. Right now we have not isolated the problem well enough. FCM has done a tremendous job, but its lobbying has fallen on deaf ears. Each and every year they say: "We want you to address the problem." Some minister says: "We will listen. We are good listeners", but nothing ever has happened. I do not suspect, judging from what the member for Anjou-Riviere-des-Prairies said today, there is any help forthcoming.
I would strongly encourage the government to initiate a department, not armed with millions of dollars, but one to bring about constructive dialogue. I think all Canadians, 100 per cent of the population of this country, would agree that there is a necessity for discussion about this major problem and how we are to address it. We cannot continually say, "It is not my problem". It is everyone's problem.
I have clippings that point out and isolate difficulties in so many municipalities across this country. It did not take a task force for me to find this out. We in the New Democratic Party do not have the funds to be traipsing across the country, nor do we have the funds that the government has to be everywhere. However, we are very aware of the problem. Some of the situations we read about in this country are appalling, to say the least.
Paradise, Newfoundland, for example, is a town of 4,000 people, 10 minutes from St. John's. Only 20 per cent of Paradise is served with water and sewer. They would require about $8 million from government to provide full service. They are getting $50,000 right now.

Old pipelines avenge their neglect. A good example is Yellowknife where they put in a sewer system in 1940 made of corrugated metal lined with moss for insulation. It is still functioning in the 1990s. That is amazing. That goes to show that old things that were built are still the best. We plan now for obsolescence. Plumbers tell us that they have to make repairs now that never were necessary 20 years ago. The old sewer systems are still working but they are starting to fall apart. What they found was that this system looked not unlike a fish's skeleton. The total bill now to replace this skeleton in Yellowknife is $15 million, and the saga continues.
I want to give my hon. friend from Ottawa credit. He went out to St. John's and he found out some very startling information that all of us certainly do appreciate.
"No big fix, but Clark will talk", this is 1988, Mr. Speaker, so FCM was still optimistic at that time. Everybody again seems to agree that this begs tri-level involvement.
"Municipal services", the Finance Minister says, "are the business of the federal government", pardon me, they are "no business of the federal government". I almost came upon a quotation that even would have surprised me.
Time.

Madam Speaker, I was beginning to wonder if I was ever going to be able to give
May 25, 1990

this speech. After you work on a speech late at night you begin to wonder if your speech really is a barn-burner.
I am very pleased to be able to speak on Canada's deteriorating infrastructure, and as co-chair of the Liberal task force that travelled across Canada in 1989, the critical state was very clearly brought home to me and my colleagues.
On many occasions since 1984 representations have been made to the federal government for the creation of a program to shore up Canada's deteriorating infrastructure. These proposals to date have been ignored by this government.
The facts remain, however, that without a major infusion of funds for the preservation and expansion of bridges, watermains, roads and sewers in Canada, both the productivity and safety of all Canadians will be jeopardized. A Canada-wide infrastructure program would create more jobs than the trade deal alone. It would help develop every region of the country rather than bail out corporations in select communities as this government has done.
PCBs, global warming, wildlife protection, acid rain, ozone depletion and toxic wastes are just a few of the words and catch phrases with which we Canadians are becoming all too familiar. Every day when I watch or read the news I become more and more concerned about living in a world in which the dangers posed by a deteriorating environment and the attendant economic health and social stresses are becoming very serious.
All Canadians want a bright future on this planet for their children, and in my case my grandchildren. To do this we must make global environmental security a cornerstone of Canada's policy.
Historically all three levels of government; municipal, provincial, and federal, have contributed to the costs of financing urban infrastructure. From 1938 to 1984 the federal government made funds available for infrastructure programs. Some of the programs included, from 1938 to 1949, the Municipal Improvement Assistance Act; 1961 to 1974, the Sewage Treatment Program; 1963 to 1966, Municipal Development and Loan Act; 1973 to 1979, the Neighbourhood Improvement Program; 1975 to 1978, the Municipal Infrastructure Program; and 1979 to 1980, the Community Services Contribution Program.
Supply
In those years the governments of Canada had been very committed to the infrastructure of this country. Today's federal government has refused to accept any share of the responsibility for infrastructure, leaving the municipal and provincial governments to struggle with this increasing financial burden.
The government argues that constitutionally they have no responsibility in the areas of infrastructure. It is, however, very important to note that the Constitution does not provide for federal involvement in health care, education or social services, yet they are involved as a major contributor in all these areas. Therefore, how can the federal government deny its responsibility for the environment, clean water, regional and national economic development?
The federal government is not only a badly needed funding partner but it is also in the best position to co-ordinate the establishment of national standards and goals.
The favourite statement coming from the government side of the House these days, and they seem to deliver this statement with great gusto and pleasure, is, "Where is the money going to come from?" Well, I have a few ideas of where it can come from. But in order to provide the minimum national standard of service, intergovernmental funding transfers are required. The federal government is in the best position to co-ordinate the establishment of national standards and goals, and the government often states that cities need only raise their water rates to pay for the rehabilitation of their infrastructure. This is certainly one method and it is certainly done by many municipalities across this country.
However, the water costs of some cities would amount to more than the property taxes in order to generate the revenues required. These are all in areas of the country where they can least afford it. Water rates are only one method. There is another method of user-pay that could be utilized in areas where there are severely neglected roads and bridges. These could be rehabilitated with fees from the users of the transportation system.
The federal government is currently levying heavy taxes on the users of gasoline and diesel fuel but channels none of these revenues into our road systems.

May 25, 1990

Three, investors will choose particular areas of Canada because of the quality of life and the services the area provides. Investment, in turn, creates jobs and increased assessment for the city, resulting in a flourishing economy.
Four, in depressed regions of Canada an infusion of regional development dollars reduces the UIC and welfare costs and puts people back to work. The old saying of "a dollar spent is a dollar earned" is borne out in this instance.
I would like to comment on a few of the cities or areas of Canada that we visited. In the Vancouver area witnesses stressed that the federal government must stop this ad hocery of repairing Canada's infrastructure. They cited examples of the $200 million spent on the Halifax harbour, which certainly will not clean up the Halifax harbour unless sewage treatment plants are in place. There is the example of the infusion of money along the St. Lawrence River which just happened to be at election time. They said this country is in economic chaos due to crisis mismanagement.
Those were the comments from the city of Vancouver. The pulp mills of British Columbia must be cleaned up and wood preservatives eliminated. Global warming is the number two issue in the world and is closely tied to poor infrastructure due to the regulations.
In Nova Scotia, sewage treatment plants are a rarity. People have to carry their drinking water. Open sewers running into ditches are commonplace.
The lack of services destroy the potential of essential growth. The rural areas of Nova Scotia we visited indicated they are always ignored in favour of big towns and cities such as Dartmouth or Halifax.
The Village of Little Narrows in Nova Scotia has never had potable water. The town of Dominion has a moratorium on development. They cannot meet requests for development due to an inadequate system.
Seven outlets in Cape Breton are pumping raw sewage parallel to one of the finest beaches on Cape Breton Island. Tourism is affected. Listening to witnesses speak about such desolation, one wonders whether we are we really talking about Canada or about a Third World country? But, it is surely Canada.
In Newfoundland they stress four points very strongly. There is a need for access to clean water by all Canadians. There is a need for adequate sewage treatment facilities. There is a need for safe roads and bridges, and there is a need for intergovernmental cost sharing.
As the Mayor of Conception Bay said: "An improved infrastructure would create a cleaner and safer environment, would strengthen the economy of the island of Newfoundland and would expand their standard of living".
We heard from the St. Lawrence Seaway cites of Cornwall and Kingston. Mayor Poirier of Cornwall said the responsibility for infrastructure and its deterioration is accelerating at a rate they can no longer afford.
Mayor Cooper of Kingston said the province of Ontario has ordered them to stop issuing building permits until they upgrade their facilities. Economic survival is the issue.
In northern Ontario, the Mayor of North Bay said it is time the federal government realized that this is not a local issue but a national issue.
All the cities and towns in northern Ontario stress the inadequacy of the Trans-Canada Highway. Truckers cannot compete with their American counterpart, travel time is longer, highway fuel consumption is higher. The young people of the north are moving south. The single-lane highway is alienating the north from the southern portion of Ontario. An adequate four-lane highway with same day delivery to Thunder Bay, Toronto or Detroit will make them far more competitive. In Thunder Bay, the cost of a secondary sewage treatment plant alone will bankrupt the city.
The water system in the nation's capital in the national capital region is a pay as you go system. Over the next 10 years, $10 billion must be spent and raised to cover capital dollars for sewage treatment and water expansion. Maybe people from outside this region will know that there are 10 municipalities that make up the Ottawa-Carleton region and that the city of Ottawa is one of them. In this city alone 18 overflows from the heritage sewers are going directly into the Ottawa River, not to mention the very sensitive nature of the Rideau River and its inherent problems.
May 25, 1990

I have only mentioned a few of the regions in the country, but everywhere the task force visited and in the regions that wrote, the story was abysmal. Only 10 per cent of all raw sewage east of Ontario is treated. Government members should listen to this: only 10 per cent of all raw sewage east of Ontario is treated. More than 8 million Canadians or one-third of the entire population of this country live in municipalities that do not provide sewage treatment. Water quality in Toronto is causing so much concern that some politicians are calling for a $200 million pipeline from Georgian Bay to serve the city.
The value of a water treatment and delivery system now totals a staggering $100 billion. The bill for the next five years for repairing aging, underground pipes alone has been estimated at $3 billion. No level of government in Canada is budgeting for rehabilitation programs of that magnitude.
Beyond speech making from the government side of this House, we have so far seen little federal commitment to the environment. Our rivers and our harbours are polluted from Halifax to Vancouver. Beaches are closed, summer after summer, because the federal government does not make sewer construction and repair a national priority. It is ironic that under the Great Lakes action plan the federal government has recently announced a $125 million fund for the restoration and preservation of this vital water system; this in addition to the almost $1 billion already spent by the government on the Great Lakes since 1972. Yet we are still pumping raw sewage into the Great Lakes system.
There is a cost of doing business. The transportation of goods and services is one important cost to business. Roads in poor condition increase costs, not only through increased use of fuel but through deterioration of vehicles and lost time. Poor roads and lack of waste disposal facilities also add to the costs of businesses, either through increased dump fees or increased costs to have their own waste hauled away. As governments at all levels start placing stricter environmental controls and ask business to bear the costs of its own pollution, business will be able to operate more efficiently in communities that have the infrastructure to handle and treat waste water.
Now that we know Canadians are the least energy efficient consumers in the world. Every possible method
Supply
has to be used to improve our record through sustainable development. The cost of cleaning up our damaged rivers and lakes far exceeds the cost of treating sewage before it gets to these rivers and lakes. Polluters to date have remained unpunished, and the federal government has failed to prosecute a single polluter in Ontario during the past year. The failure to go after polluters has occurred, even though Ottawa has the Canadian Environmental Protection Act which carries a maximum penalty of $1 million.
No single action will be enough to ensure the future health and viability of Canada's infrastructure. A broad range of measures is necessary to make a meaningful difference. Specifically, these should include the following: a federal recognition of municipal infrastructure as a crisis of national proportions; a federal commitment to share the responsibility to rebuild infrastructure with its provincial and municipal counterparts; the establishment of minimum national standards for infrastructure to provide that environmental protection and uniform levels of service for all Canadians; a federal commitment to rehabilitate and expand the Trans-Canada Highway; the establishment of a process through which the federal government can clarify the respective roles of federal, provincial and municipal governments; identify and prio-rize needs on a national scale; increase incentives for maintenance and reconstruction of existing capital assets and the use of low capital; explore alternative funding sources, including such options as more rational user fees for water services; applying fuel tax revenues to road construction and maintenance and increased private sector involvement; increase support for research and development to accelerate technological innovation; promote more efficient municipal management methods to permit phased programs of rehabilitation, better management of infrastructure systems, and more effective use of funds and to reduce waste and excess costs due to delays.
It has been a great privilege for me to travel across the country and talk to Canadians. I heard the desolate response and comments expressed to us in the Liberal task force on Canada's infrastructure.
I have always maintained that everyone in Canada has a right to a roof over their head, food on their table and the very basic amenities of life. Water is probably the

May 25, 1990
Supply
most important one, and sewage treatment is probably second.
How can we sit here in the Parliament of Canada when only 10 per cent of the people east of Ontario have adequate facilities? It is shameful and it is disgraceful. The member for Sault Ste. Marie criticized me, sitting on this side of the House, for being concerned about my fellow Canadians and am trying to do something about it. I would applaud him if he was doing the same. As Canadians, we have got to be aware of the inequities in our system and we must do something about it.
I have thrown the government several ideas on how this can be financed. It is high time we recognized the difference between expenditure and investment. This is an investment in Canada's people; it is an investment in our future, in our children, and in our grandchildren.
As I mentioned earlier, more jobs then under the free trade agreement will be created through this program. I see my colleague here in the House. What could be better for the town of Canso, Nova Scotia, where there was the closure of fish plants, than creating a regional development program in that area. It could put those same people, who have been laid off due to the closure of the fish plants, to work. The same situation exists in Newfoundland. It is not expending government funds because it will be paid back in spades. It will get paid back in jobs, through economic development and the cancellation of welfare and UIC.
It is high time that the government recognized that there are Canadians that are probably less fortunate than we in the House. We have a responsibility as legislators to ensure that Canadians are not living in a third-world type of environment.

speakeroldname: Mr. John A. MacDougall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in listening to the hon. member's comments, one would almost think that all the devastation that she portrays has happened since 1984.
As someone involved in municipal politics for a number of years before being elected to the House-and I know that she has served for a period of time on municipal council as well-I find it regrettable that she does not realize that municipalities have a great responsibility in budgeting their money and in being able to^put
funds aside for upgrading and for water and sewer projects.
The community I came from made certain each year we had the opportunity to advance that responsibility for better drinking water and sewer projects. But politicians at the municipal level do not like that because it is under the ground. They would sooner be putting tennis courts and arenas in, things above the ground, because that gets them re-elected.
We should be dealing with realities and I wish the hon. member would start to deal with reality. The reality is that we started in 1984 as a government and the programs were discontinued by her government back in 1980. She said that 10 per cent of eastern Canada is without sufficient water and sewage. It is very regrettable when she tries to blame this Party and this government for those problems.
I say to the hon. member that she should get her facts straight and remember history. That party was in power for 20 years under great economic times. If she goes back in history, she will see the number of infrastructures put in place in industrial parks that are sitting today with not a thing in them and where federal dollars were spent.
How can she say to the House in all sincerity that the infrastructure problems are a federal issue when she knows quite clearly it belongs to the provinces and the municipalities? I really want to know why she thinks it should be the federal government's responsibility when the responsibility lies with the provinces and municipalities.

Madam Speaker, the member's statement sounds very simplistic, but it is not that simple.
The programs were in place all of the years that I mentioned. Canada was gradually trying to get out of the trap the municipalities were in. They were making headway. The program has been cancelled since 1982. Does that mean to say that because the program was cancelled by a Liberal government in 1982, it is no reason why I, as a Liberal, would not want to reinstate the program? Come on now.
The member probably comes from a municipality, such as I do, where municipal sewers are up to date. We have arenas, we have everything, because my municipality is well off and his is probably well off, too. But there are eastern municipalities that could not even pay the
May 25, 1990

one-third share. When we said to them, if the federal government pays one-third and the province one-third, can you pay your one-third? They could not pay it.
Travel around the country a little bit and see what is there. Open your eyes. Open your eyes and see what is out there.
Why could they not pay it?

They cannot because they do not have job creation, the tax base and the wealth in their municipalities that you and I have.
I find the comment of the member absolutely unconscionable. There is a serious, serious problem in this country. Is the hon. member serious about the environment in this country? For instance, if a city or a town 50 miles down the river is dumping raw sewage into the river, why is that the problem of the municipality 50 miles upriver? It is not, it is a much bigger problem than that. It is a provincial and federal problem.
I fail to understand the insensitivity of the member opposite. I find that regrettable. I am sure the people across the country will find that a very insensitive comment.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to participate in this debate. I got quite excited about getting involved with this when I heard what we would be discussing this afternoon.
We are discussing a motion by a member of the Liberal party that asks the federal government to recognize the crisis that exists in municipal infrastructure. The motion indicates that the problem is serious and affects the nation's environment, economic prosperity and quality of life for Canadians.
Everyone is for quality of life and prosperity of Canadians. When it comes to municipal infrastructure, most of us agree with all the different components that go into making a healthy municipal infrastructure; that bridges are a good thing in municipalities, that water mains are a good idea. We all want good sewage treatment facilities and good local transportation. We all want street lights that work on every street in our community. We all agree with these things, and I would not want anyone to misinterpret any of my future
Supply
comments on the subject. I agree. I want to see good lights on the street where I live, I want to see good sewage treatment, good water mains, garbage pick-up. I want all those things.
What we are really talking about here and what this motion addresses is really the subject of money and who should pay it. It was made very clear by the Liberal party and the New Democratic speakers today that a great chunk of that must come from the federal government, not just the billions of dollars that we transfer now and put into areas that are of benefit to the municipalities, not just what we are doing now, but far more.
One member thundered "the fair share of the federal government." A recent speaker said "the one-third traditional share the federal government pays for areas"-areas which I might add are within municipal and provincial jurisdiction, not federal jurisdiction, exclusively within the jurisdiction of the provinces and the municipalities.
The members of the Liberal party and the NDP thunder "The federal government must pay its fair share, the federal government must pay one-third of these things."
Madam Speaker, I think you and I both know what would happen if a resolution or bill was introduced by the federal government asking the municipalities and the provincial government to pick up a third of federal programs. I think you know the answer to that one. The NDP would scream: "We will bring Parliament to its knees. How dare the federal government suggest that anything in the federal area would be paid for by the provincial and municipal governments." I can see them nodding their heads in agreement. They would fight that to the very end. That would be a terrible thing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Thank you, Madam Speaker. To be fair to the hon. member, I would be very pleased to know how they would feel about the sharing of all services across the country, and particularly my hypothetical suggestion as to what the reaction of the New Democratic Party would be if we suggested that to the municipalities and provinces. If I am mistaken and they might welcome something like that, I would be very pleased to hear it. I know that the debate will go on for a little bit longer and I would be very pleased if they would address that question.
One of the things in the speeches of the Liberals and the NDP is that there is no mention of the national debt. There is unanimity that the federal government should be spending more money in the areas of municipal jurisdiction. That is unanimous on the other side, but there is no suggestion about the problems of debt. Particularly silent on this of course are the members of the Liberal party because they were the ones who engineered, orchestrated and made up the debt that we are experiencing today.
The hon. member from Hamilton knows that. He knows that when we came to office in 1984 the debt was over $200 billion. He knows that the interest on that puts it well over $300 billion. There is no discussion from the Liberal party as to the national debt in this or in any other forum. The one thing they are very sure of is that they want to spend more money. Well, that is certainly in order from their past performances in this area.
At the same time you do not hear that there is any problem with the national debt, they are unanimous on the subject of tax increases.
On many occasions I heard members of the NDP talk to Parliament about 31 increases in taxes since the Tories came to power. The Liberals have said the same thing. Presumably, they are against those tax increases. They talk about them all the time. They disagree with the number of tax increases.
I always point out that five of those are in the area of increases in the tax on tobacco. Surely that has something to do with the quality of life, but I take the NDP at their word. If they are against all tax changes that the Tories have made in the last six years, I accept that. I disagree with it, because again, it is not coming to reality. It is not coming to grips with the problems that this country is suffering.
What we are talking about here is a question of philosophy. In all these areas, the members of the opposition are not satisfied that anybody else is doing anything or that anybody can be responsible for anything else except the federal government. If it is municipal services, the federal government should pay more. If it is within provincial jurisdiction, the federal government should pay more.
On many occasions, I and other members have pointed out that these are areas within exclusive provincial jurisdiction. They say: "Show leadership. Set national standards. You get in. You take over the area." If it is in the private sector, they say the same thing. It is not good enough to have the private sector ever look after anything, because the federal government should be laying down the law, setting the standards. Above all and most important, it should pay.
As an example, yesterday, I was very pleased during the debate to hear a fine expression of NDP philosophy when it comes to paying. The subject was pre-marital counselling. I challenge an hon member of the NDP to look it up on page 11815 of Hansard. Here is what he asked Parliament. You may remember this, Madam Speaker.
Do we do any pre-marital counselling in the country? Not a whit.
No, there is no chance. On the next page he goes on to say that the state at least can make, among other things, pre-marital counselling available. That is the problem. The state is not paying for it.
It was pointed out to the hon. member that there are many voluntary agencies involved with pre-marital counselling. When it is pointed out to the hon. member or the members of the NDP that the churches and other groups in this country are very involved with pre-marital counselling, it does not count at all. The hon. member says: "Not a whit." It does not exist if the federal government, the state, is not paying for it.
May 25, 1990

That is the philosophy of the members of the New Democratic Party when it comes to anything in the private sector. It is the same as we see in the debate today when it comes to areas within exclusive federal and provincial jurisdiction.
One good example of this is the subject of day care, an area within exclusive provincial jurisdiction and one into which the federal government, quite rightly, pours hundreds of billions of dollars through the Canada Assistance Program. We provide tax benefits through the Income Tax Act to help middle income Canadians afford day care. But it is not enough for the members of the New Democratic Party.
I was sitting with the hon. member for Erie on a child care task force a couple of years ago, and he started listening to all the different ideas that the NDP had in the area of provincial jurisdiction. He said to me: "I think what the NDP is proposing is going to cost about $20 billion." He said: "The NDP must have a real big bank account to pay for all of this." Except for the part that I know they do not like banks, I knew the point he was trying to make, that it is not good enough that the federal government contribute as it is doing. It is never enough if it is in an area of provincial jurisdiction.
I challenged a group of students on one of the things in this area. I had the pleasure to be at Governor Simcoe High School in St. Catharines a couple of weeks ago discussing the subject of the GST. There were the usual groups who are against the GST. They are fighting the GST. Of course, they were very weak I thought in the areas as to what we would come up with for alternatives, or how we would balance the budget.
I threw out a challenge to the students of that school. I said: "I have sat in Parliament for six years." I challenged the members of that high school and I challenge the members of this House: Pick up Hansard from any day within the last six years and come up with one day that the NDP has not been suggesting that we spend more money that we do not have in some other area. What day did they not want to spend more of the government's money? That is the challenge I issued to them.
I ask the hon. member to find me a Hansard of the last six years where the NDP was not advocating that we spend more money on top of the national debt that

exists. The NDP and Liberal philosophy is just more, more and more.
The NDP, quite apart from their enthusiastic support of this Liberal motion for increased municipal infrastructure costs, has asked in the last few months for more money for the Post Office to abolish supermailboxes. They want a youth initiative program for $1.5 billion. They want the federal government to start spending more money on UIC. They want to increase foreign aid, increase the child tax credits, increase the spousal allowances, more money to CBC, and more money on social housing.
I was just talking with the Minister of State for Housing. We put $1.8 billion into housing. Of course, if you sit in the opposition, money is no problem. It is never enough. It should be doubled and quadrupled. Ten billion dollars is not enough for day care, it should be $20 billion for day care.
Our friends in the Liberal party are not far behind. They want more for all the things the NDP want, plus agriculture, post-secondary education, housing, spousal allowances, research and development, and on and on in a country that has a $350 billion debt, and at a time when the government is honestly, with the taxpayers' money, trying to come to grips with this problem.
You heard what was described as a lover's quarrel here recently, Madam Speaker, as to whether the Liberals used to pay for municipal infrastructure. On this debate on that particular quarrel, I want to tell you that I side with the Liberals.

I was just about to say, before I was interrupted, that that is one area where I actually agree with the Liberals. I do not think there is any area the NDP could mention that there were not federal Liberal dollars going into before 1984.
There is one point I want to make about that spending and it is on the subject of municipal infrastructure. In my riding of Niagara Falls, I am very pleased to have a secondary water pollution control plant. The announcement for that and the commitment of the federal government was made by the previous government prior to 1984. Out of $12 million, I believe that the federal commitment was $4 million. The government changed in 1984 and the commitment, of course, remained. I was very pleased to go to the opening of this plant.
One municipal politician said to me that it was the Liberals who promised us the money for this. I said that that was true, but that it would be the Conservative Minister of Finance who will figure out where the money is coming from. What do you get more credit for? The Liberals were using the national credit card for all those years, and it was smoking in those months before 1984. A lot of credit has to go the the Minister of Finance. It is his job to pay for those municipal infrastructures that were promised by the previous government. He is the one who is going to have to figure it out. He is doing a marvellous job. All Canadians should applaud that.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I see that my time is just about over.
More, more.

Thank you. If I have the unanimous consent of the House to continue, I would certainly be pleased to do so.
The government took office in 1984, as you will remember, Madam Speaker. The Minister of Labour indicated to the House this morning that at that time there was a $16 billion operating deficit left over. Of course that is as a result of those spending practices I made mention of a minute ago.
The great thing about the finances of this country, and this was mentioned in the The Economic Prosperity of Canada, obviously a pretty important component of that is the government's ability to turn that operating deficit around into an operating surplus. If it had not been for that deficit that we inherited in 1984, we would have more money for all those wonderful projects that we have heard about every single day for the last six years coming from the opposition. We would have had more money for them, if we had not overspent in the 1970s and the early 1980s.
You've doubled it since with your incompetence.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
All of us want all the good things in life. We all want everything from better pensions, more social services to better street lights. It is always just a question, in my opinion, of who should pay for them.
Madam Speaker, you have heard the member who introduced the motion. He is from Ontario, as I am. The situation in Ontario is that Queen's Park runs at a surplus. For the last two budgets it has run at a surplus. They make money down at Queen's Parks. All municipalities in Ontario, in his province, are required not to operate at a deficit.
There is a situation of areas within exclusive municipal and provincial jurisdiction where the decision has been made. Members of the NDP know that municipalities have to operate on a break-even basis. The member who introduced the motion knows that his own province is running at a surplus now. He has decided: "No. The best one to pay for municipal and provincial services is, of
May 25, 1990

course, the federal government". It is $350 billion in debt".
The member for Carleton-Gloucester had a rallying cry. He said: "There are 60 former municipal politicians in this House. They should all get behind this thing". I can tell the members opposite that when you come to the House of Commons you are not here to be lobbying on behalf of municipal councils. You are here for the best interests of all Canadians.
Members of the opposition say: "Do not raise taxes. Do not make cuts. Spend a lot more. The deficit is your problem". That is not a recipe that I think Canadians are going to buy. I do not think it is ultimately going to sell. I think, ultimately, that is why the Progressive Conservatives are on this side of the House and they have for many years now been on that side of the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On question or comments, the hon. member for Victoria.

Madam Speaker, while the member was going on we had a vote among members on this side of the House. We decided we would award the member the prize for the best high school debater in this debate so far.
He has waxed enthusiastic, but he has missed the fundamental point, which is that there has been a long tradition in this country of federal government leadership when national programs are necessary.
Even his own government has provided funds for sewage treatment in Halifax and Quebec City, for example. It has provided funds for municipal infrastructure, but on an ad hoc basis so that it can dole it out at the time of election campaigns.
What is important about the proposal of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities is that there be a planned national campaign in partnership with all levels of government which recognizes the responsibilities of all levels of government, not just for municipal services, but for the rivers, lakes and oceans into which sewage is flowing because of the antiquated system we have in this country.
This debate and the speech of the hon. member gives me an opportunity to bring to the attention of the House the situation in my own area in greater Victoria. Over 100 years of growth in the area has been accompanied by
Supply
a failure to keep up with the disposal of waste that grows in industrial areas.
In this sense we are in common in keeping with so many other municipalities. We have sewage disposal facilities, but they were developed 20 and 30 years ago, and in some cases much longer ago than that. It was an age when we were far less conscious of the requirements to keep a clean environment and not to make the environment any worse for what we have taken from it.
Clearly, what has been identified now in our community is a requirement that we stop pumping raw sewage into the ocean. It is an ocean which, I may say, comes under federal jurisdiction. The federal government clearly has a responsibility in this area, as it recognized in the case of Halifax where it put up $100 million to clean up Halifax harbour. If it can do that for Halifax and Quebec City, then it can do it for Victoria and for other communities across the country.
I am surprised in fact now to hear the government speaking against it. When the Prime Minister came into our area during the last election campaign he was not against it. Conservatives in our area who ran-unfortunately for them a losing cause, but they still ran and put up a good fight-committed the Conservative Party and for those who vote for it to a federal-provincial-municipal infrastructure campaign.
I fail to understand how those who are close to the government are here speaking against this motion.
The capital regional district did a study recently.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member mentioned the Halifax harbour clean-up, as well as that of the St. Lawrence. I can mention to him as well money going into the Niagara area and the Great Lakes area as well-in fact into all areas of pollution.

May 25, 1990
Supply
I agree with the hon. member on this. The problems of pollution are not within any particular level of government's exclusive jurisdiction. It is all our responsibility.
One member of the Liberal party even commended the government for spending money in Elalifax and some other of these areas. I guess that is the point.
The federal government is involved. We transfer billions of dollars to the provincial governments. We have many joint projects, everything from the environment to agriculture. I mentioned the Minister of State for Housing, who is to my right, who committed $1.8 billion a year to housing, these are substantial sums of money.
One of the things that the members of the New Democratic Party never seem to realize is that all of them are great ideas-all of them. It is always just a question of how much money and how quickly we can put money into these worth-while projects.
As I say, I am quite sure that for members of the NDP $1.8 billion is not enough for housing. I am sure $3.6 billion, $7.4 and $14 billion is not half enough for the members of the NDP. But the responsibility of the Minister of Finance is to balance the very legitimate concerns of all Canadians and all areas, and at the same time try to ensure that the Government of Canada does not end up bankrupt trying to do it.

Madam Speaker, the member has discussed the role of federal involvement in what may be interpreted as being both municipal and provincial matters. He has reflected upon the fact that in many cases, as it may be perceived, the federal government may in fact be overstepping its jurisdiction. That might actually be the case, if it were a matter that the federal government came in against the wishes of the provinces or the municipalities. The member knows full well that both municipalities and provinces throughout Canada had been requesting strong federal initiatives in terms of the assistance required in developing municipal infrastructure, particularly in the areas of waste management and water management. I want to point out to the member that his own government has, in fact, recognized the need for this type of initiative.
I remind him of the federal government's water policy which was tabled in 1987. It states that "the federal government intends to work with the provinces and
territories to encourage the provision of safe and sufficient water supplies for Canadians". That is a quote right out of the federal water policy. It goes on to state that the over-all goal of the federal water policy is to "encourage the use of freshwater in an efficient and equitable manner, consistent with social, cultural and environmental needs". It then identifies two major objectives to achieve that goal: To protect and enhance the quality of the water resource, both in supply and disposal; and, to promote the wise and efficient use of water.
This is a stated initiative in the federal water policy of the government to get involved at the regional and provincial levels with assistance for such programs as water supply and waste management.
It is beyond me to sit and listen to the arguments presented by the member on the government side that this is not a federal responsibility when in fact this very same government has made those initiatives and committed itself, I might add, to do such.
I will extend the argument one more step. Although that has been stated in the federal water policy document, I might provide further evidence for the benefit of the member that that document continues to be a vacuous philosophical tool. It can be used by this government but has no legislation to back it up.
We on this side of the House say that it is time the government put its money where its mouth is. It has made that commitment to the provinces and to the regions within those provinces to get involved in the problems of water management, water supply and waste disposal. It is right there in the document. The member must recognize that.
The government has to recognize that, if it wants to maintain the quality of life that Canadians are used to throughout the country, it has to take the bull by the horns. It has to get involved in these kinds of initiatives that will maintain the environmental quality, not only of our oceans, but of our lakes and inland waters which are also being affected by waste and untreated sewage.

The millions of dollars that we are spending in the Great Lakes is for clean water. The money that is being spent in Halifax is for clean water. We are doing those things. We have done them in the past.
We are even trying to pay for the ones that were done before 1984, the ones that were all on the credit card. We will pay for those and we will pay for the ones that we are doing at the present time, as well as those we will do in the future.

Madam Speaker, the opposition motion now under consideration reads as follows:
That this House call upon the government to recognize that Canada's municipal infrastructure is facing a crisis of national proportions and that, given the serious implications to the nation's environment, economic prosperity and quality of life for Canadians, the government resume its traditional role as a partner with the provincial and municipal governments to address this national crisis.
I would suggest that any Canadian familiar with the municipal infrastructure issue will agree with this motion.
First, Madam Speaker, I want to congratulate two of my colleagues who created and worked with this task force, the hon. member for Nepean (Mrs. Gaffney) and the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Harb).
Naturally each of us in his or her respective region was glad to co-operate and work with municipal councils to examine infrastructures, budgets, and improvements to be undertaken. The mayors and municipal councillors in my riding of Gatineau-La Lievre were invited to attend and, much to my surprise, the most pressing issue was the funding required to make improvements or, at the very least, upgrade of the municipal infrastructure to acceptable levels. This makes you think, of course. But
Supply
when we consider the amounts required for one Canadian region alone it soon becomes patently clear that there has been a lot of negligence over the years, no matter which government was in office at the time. It is so obvious that I had to reflect upon the matter.
Four or five years ago, as I was reading letters to the editor in the well-known New York Times, I spotted an article by a professor of the highly respected Columbia University who had made an exhaustive study throughout the United States-their situation can be compared to ours, I would think-and concluded that the American municipal infrastructure situation was alarming. Not worrisome, alarming! Roadways, bridges and municipal infrastructures generally were in an unbelieveble state of disrepair, and this was four or five years ago. They say the bill to upgrade infrastructures would amount to something like $500 billion, if you can imagine! This gives you an idea of what needs to be done to bring municipal infrastructures up to more satisfactory levels. Nor can we ignore the fact that there has been negligence.
I remember that spokesmen for the Union des municipality du Quebec came to Ottawa to meet members of the various caucuses. The former mayor of Quebec City was there, as were representatives of the City of Montreal, Sherbrooke and other localities. They gave us a rundown on the situation in their respective municipalities, and indeed there is cause for great concern. From all this we can only conclude that the municipal infrastructure upgrading process is a major undertaking.

I just want to bring out one point. This should be an ongoing operation. Programs should not arrive on the eve of an election. It should be an ongoing process.
I am convinced, when the whole infrastructure deteriorates to the point it is getting to now, that it even has adverse effects on the fabric of our society. I do not think that is an exaggeration. It is a fact.
It is remarkable to think that a country such as Canada has 25 per cent of all the fresh water in the world and the Province of Quebec has 15 per cent of all the fresh water in the world. Yet we are beginning to see problems concerning the supply of fresh water. Can one imagine what is going on in the rest of the world? How did we get to this point?

We must say that the way in which we have handled waste management and sewage treatment has compounded our problems. Therefore, when it comes to municipal infrastructure, regardless of the government, the federal government, which obviously has the resources, along with the provincial and municipal governments, should form a team. We should not say that the provincial government will have precedence over the federal government or vice versa. It is a joint effort, and it is extremely important. I am sure that Canadians from coast to coast are concerned about it.
I do not think it is a surprise to say that the environment and the infrastructure go hand in hand.
We have seen this neglect over the years. We are coming to the point where we are going to have to reconsider how we have handled the whole situation of municipal infrastructure.
It can be said that, if it gets to this point of deterioration, then it practically comes under peace, order, and good government. It is such an essential element for all our municipalities and towns that we cannot let it become the whim of political parties. They cannot say, on the eve of elections, that they are going to invest x number of billions of dollars.

Madam Speaker, I remember the early 1970s when I had the pleasure to represent the riding of Papineau in the National Assembly. It was a time of great prosperity. We had funds at our disposal. I remember that they were good years in that regard and we ended each year without a deficit, even for current expenditures. At that time, we invested in municipal infrastructure, but maybe not enough. I remember the sewers, viaducts, aqueducts and so on. If a good part of this country's deficit had been for our municipal infrastructure, it would be much easier for us to take.
There has been neglect and we have come to a point where it is essential for all levels of government to join together. We must look into this issue because, as I said, it affects the very structure of our society. It is extremely important for it to be an ongoing process of making sure that municipal infrastructure throughout Canada will never again be neglected. Every municipality must have a continuing stock of municipal infrastructure not only for the security of our fellow citizens but for a healthy
environment, which definitely affects our human behaviour.
There is nothing magic about that, except that it is always a matter of having the necessary political will. People expect us to take such initiatives. It will obviously be very expensive but there are choices to be made and this one is a priority in a modem society like ours which needs the technology.
In closing, Madam Speaker, I hope this motion will encourage every political party in this House to develop a policy on the municipal infrastructure issue, not to buy votes but to assess with objectivity the situation across the country and make a commitment not to let it deteriorate as it has done in the past 20 years.

Madam Speaker, I listened to my Liberal colleague and I think that a lot of his arguments are most pertinent.
I think he would agree with my comments that, in large measure, the government has been preoccupied with the big ticket items that have been facing the country: free trade; the GST; and, now, trying to put spit and polish on its Constitution, wringing its hands over the situation with the Meech Lake Accord. Meanwhile, while we are looking at these big ticket items, it is the nuts and bolts that have continued to rust, the very problems that face our many municipalities in Canada. I think the member would also agree that the government has been pleading poverty, faced with a terrible, burdensome debt.
Yet, the member knows as well as any member in the House that during the last election this same government promised the taxpayers of Canada some $20 billion in election goodies. That is what the price-tag was, $20 billion. Read my lips.
After the election, we are suddenly faced with a terrible debt. But during the election, the Minister of Finance never even recognized that there was a debt problem.
